Abstract—Illegal logging is a primary driver of global de-
forestation, causing significant biodiversity loss and accelerating
carbon emissions. Traditional surveillance methods are limited:
optical satellite imaging suffers from cloud cover and low
temporal resolution, while bioacoustic networks generate high
false-alarm rates due to complex forest biophony and require
high-bandwidth streaming of raw audio to centralized servers,
raising severe privacy concerns. This paper proposes Forest
Guardian AI, a decentralized, multi-modal edge framework for
real-time threat detection. By deploying a lightweight Audio-
CNN for in-situ acoustic classification and a ResNet-34 based
U-Net for satellite image segmentation at the edge, the system
implements a robust ”ears and eyes” late-fusion mechanism. A
cross-modal Boolean veto gate requires simultaneous acoustic
threat detection (e.g., chainsaw or engine) and localized satellite-
detected canopy loss (> 5%) before escalating a critical alert. To
address data privacy and bandwidth limitations, we incorporate
Federated Learning (FL) using the Flower framework with the
Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm. Experimental results
demonstrate an acoustic classification accuracy of 95.7%, a visual
segmentation Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.857, and a
federated global accuracy of 92.3%. Critically, the cross-modal
veto logic reduces the false-alarm rate from 25.4% to 4.2%,
while the FL protocol reduces data transmission overhead by
95.8% compared to raw audio streaming, making continuous
environmental defense technically and economically feasible on
resource-constrained solar-powered edge hardware.

solution for environmental monitoring. Fusing acoustic and

approach: the U-Net filters out transient acoustic noise, and the

The system uses a late-fusion ”ears and eyes” veto mech-
anism. A lightweight 3-layer Audio-CNN continuously mon-

To improve the edge models without centralizing raw data,
we implement Federated Learning (FL) using the Flower
framework. Nodes compute local updates to the Audio-CNN
weights and transmit these small parameter sets (≈2.36 MB)
to a central server. The server aggregates updates using the
Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm and broadcasts the
updated global model. This reduces bandwidth consumption

II. RELATED WORK
Automated bioacoustic monitoring was popularized by
projects like Rainforest Connection (RFCx) [11], which
streamed environmental audio from canopy-mounted smart-
phones to cloud servers. While useful, the reliance on cloud-
based classification is limited by network coverage and cellular
costs. Recent research has shifted toward edge computing.
Faraone et al. [12] deployed shallow SVMs and random forest
classifiers directly on microcontrollers to detect chainsaw
noise. However, these systems are vulnerable to high false-
positive rates under noisy forest conditions.
For visual monitoring, semantic segmentation networks like
U-Net [3] and DeepLab have replaced traditional vegeta-
tion index thresholding (e.g., NDVI). Combining visual and
acoustic modalities is an active area of research. Tang et al.
[13] proposed a centralized multi-modal system using satellite
change detection to prioritize acoustic sensors. However, their
architecture still relies on centralized cloud infrastructure.
Federated Learning, introduced by McMahan et al. [1],
enables collaborative training of deep models on decentralized
data. While widely used in mobile keyboards [4] and medical
imaging, its application to environmental acoustics remains
limited. Our work combines edge multi-modal late-fusion with
federated learning to build a low-power, privacy-preserving,
and bandwidth-efficient system for illegal logging detection.

A. Semantic Segmentation using ResNet-34 U-Net

1) Temporal Resolution: Revisit times range from 5 to 16
days. Illegal loggers exploit these predictable gaps to
complete ”hit-and-run” operations within 24–48 hours.
2) Cloud Occlusion: Optical imagery cannot penetrate
cloud cover, which exceeds 70% of imaging opportu-
nities in the tropics.
3) Selective Logging Detection: Free satellite imagery
(10m–30m per pixel) cannot resolve the removal of
individual high-value trees (e.g., teak, mahogany) under
an otherwise intact canopy.
B. Limitations of Centralized Acoustic Monitoring
To capture active logging, bioacoustic monitoring networks
record environmental sounds. However, traditional systems
stream raw audio continuously to central cloud servers. This
approach has two main issues:
1) Bandwidth Bottlenecks: Streaming uncompressed mono
audio at 22,050 Hz requires approximately 3.8 GB of
data per node daily. In remote forests, cellular con-
nections are unavailable, and satellite backhaul (e.g.,
Iridium SBD) is restricted to low data rates (< 1 kbps)
and is very expensive.
2) False Alarms: The forest soundscape is highly complex.
Rain on leaves, thunder, insect colonies (e.g., cicadas),
and animal calls create frequency profiles that overlap
with chainsaws, leading to high false-alarm rates (up to
25.4%) and ”alert fatigue” for rangers.
3) Privacy Concerns: Continuous recording and streaming
of raw audio risks capturing voices of indigenous pop-
ulations and forest researchers without consent.
C. The Proposed Edge-Based Multi-Modal FL Solution
To resolve these issues, we propose Forest Guardian AI,
a decentralized, multi-modal edge computing architecture. By
moving deep learning inference directly to edge devices (e.g.,
Raspberry Pi 4B), raw audio is processed locally, ensuring data
privacy and removing the need for raw data transmission.
